profiles.name: Daud Obika Tulam
profiles.description: Daud Obika Tulam, whose name was misspelled as “Daud Obida Tulam” on a widely circulated political-prisoner roster, was a New Jersey prisoner and control-unit plaintiff. His underlying 1980 convictions were for armed robbery and assault, not a political offense; as a second offender, he received an extended term of twenty to forty years. Tulam nevertheless became a politically targeted prisoner inside New Jersey State Prison. He spent eighteen years in the Management Control Unit, where prisoners were confined alone for roughly twenty-three hours a day. The American Friends Service Committee reports that New Jersey corrections officials told journalists that Tulam and two other filmed MCU prisoners had not been placed there for violating prison rules, in reporting about the political use of isolation. Tulam was released in July 2004 and later gave public testimony about the effects of prolonged isolation. His historical prisoner number was 55657; “CN-861” in the old roster was New Jersey State Prison’s mailing code, not part of that number.
profiles.finding: Justia Tulam v Beyer confirms exact identity. No verified portrait from initial search; pursue AFSC testimony footage.

profiles.name: John George Lemnitzer
profiles.description: John George Lemnitzer was a Lutheran minister born November 21, 1943 in New York City. While serving Prince of Peace Lutheran Church in Missoula, Montana, he joined the 1980 Easter peace action at Malmstrom Air Force Base. He served 90 days at the federal prison camp in Leavenworth and returned to Missoula by June 1981. Lemnitzer later served Lutheran congregations in Los Angeles, San Luis Obispo, and Phoenix. He died on October 12, 2015.

profiles.name: Bernard J. McKeon
profiles.description: Bernard “Barney” J. McKeon was born in County Leitrim, served in the United States Army from 1949 to 1951, and became a building contractor and Irish republican activist in New York. After refusing to answer a Brooklyn federal grand jury’s questions about arms shipments to Northern Ireland, he spent five months in the Metropolitan Correctional Center and was released on March 17, 1980. Indicted under the Gun Control Act in 1982, McKeon was acquitted on eight counts but convicted of conspiracy. He later served a three-year federal sentence, including time at Danbury. McKeon died in County Sligo on June 30, 1998.

profiles.name: Rita Silk Nauni
profiles.description:
Sioux and Ponca woman convicted in Oklahoma after a 1979 confrontation with Oklahoma City police in which an officer was killed while she was defending herself and her young son. Sentenced to 150 years and held at the Mabel Bassett Correctional Institution; her case became a major rallying point for Native and women's defense committees. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

Rita Silk-Nauni became a cause célèbre of the Red Power and Native rights movements after a September 1979 confrontation with Oklahoma City airport security, during which an officer was killed in what supporters described as self-defense after harassment of her and her young son. Tried before an all-white jury, she was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 150 years. Her defense committee argued she was a political prisoner subjected to abusive conditions; after a sustained campaign her sentence was reduced and she was eventually released.
profiles.finding: Ursinus Rita Silk-Nauni Defense Fund Brochure strong archive lead. Oklahoma History photograph metadc355688 explicitly depicts sister Linda Silk Heck and Frances Wise, NOT Rita; rejected.

profiles.name: Ervin Edwards
profiles.description: Ervin Edwards was prosecuted after Mobile police officer Henry Booth was killed during an August 14, 1979 struggle over Booth’s revolver. Booth had tried to arrest Edwards on an outstanding misdemeanor warrant but did not have the warrant with him. Edwards was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death. The Alabama Supreme Court later ruled that the evidence could not sustain capital murder but supported first-degree manslaughter. On December 12, 1983, the trial court entered a manslaughter judgment and imposed ten years, crediting Edwards with four years, three months, and twenty-seven days already spent in jail. The available record does not establish his eventual release date.
profiles.finding: Alabama Ex parte Edwards corroborates Henry Booth case. No identity-specific portrait verified.

profiles.name: Jerome Singleton
profiles.description: Jerome Singleton was a thirty-year-old Black student, married father of two and honorably discharged veteran when New York police arrested him in April 1979 and accused him of slashing an undercover decoy officer. Judge Bruce Wright released him on his own recognizance on April 11 after prosecutors failed to obtain an indictment within seventy-two hours. The release prompted public attacks on Wright from Mayor Ed Koch and police organizations. Singleton voluntarily returned the following day when another warrant was issued. A jury later convicted him of second-degree assault in December 1980 while acquitting him of attempted murder and first-degree assault; the sentence and any later custody have not been located.

profiles.name: Ted Clark
profiles.description: The Rev. Theodore Franklin Clark was an Atlanta civil-rights activist who joined descendants of Harris Neck, Georgia, in a campaign to reclaim land taken by the federal government during World War II. Federal marshals arrested Clark, Edgar Timmons Jr., Christopher McIntosh Jr. and Hercules Anderson at the Harris Neck National Wildlife Refuge on May 2, 1979. After a two-hour trial on May 4, the court convicted them of criminal contempt and ordered thirty days of confinement. The men spent more than fifteen days in the Savannah jail before their confinement was suspended pending appeal. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the convictions in November 1979; the exact release day and whether any remaining portion was later served have not been established.

profiles.name: Therese Coupez
profiles.description:
White anti-imperialist activist imprisoned in federal custody at FCI Pleasanton on resistance-related charges in the 1980s. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine as part of the network of North American anti-imperialist political prisoners.

Rita "Bo" Brown's partner from the Seattle area, joined the George Jackson Brigade in late 1975 and participated in numerous bombings, attempted bombings, and bank robberies in the Seattle area between January 1976 and March 1978. Arrested March 21, 1978 at a Tacoma restaurant alongside Sherman and Bertram. Convicted July 12, 1978 in W.D. Washington on Counts I-VIII (armed bank robbery, conspiracy, bombing). Sentenced to 20 years; released in 1985. Co-produced the documentary "Creating a Movement With Teeth."

profiles.name: Ronald Humphrey
profiles.description:
Ronald Louis Humphrey, born around 1936, was a United States Information Agency (USIA) foreign-service officer and the co-defendant of anti–Vietnam War activist David Truong in the 1978 Truong–Humphrey espionage case. While serving in Vietnam, Humphrey had taken a Vietnamese common-law wife, Kim; the abrupt end of the war in 1975 left her and her four children stranded in Vietnam, unable to leave.

Humphrey gave Truong USIA materials, including classified State Department diplomatic cables, which Truong passed toward the government of Vietnam. Humphrey's defense was that he acted to win the release of his common-law wife and her four children — and, he said, to support diplomatic reconciliation between the United States and Vietnam — rather than to harm the United States. Truong served as the courier; the materials were routed through an intermediary who was secretly cooperating with the FBI.

Humphrey and Truong were arrested on January 31, 1978 and charged with six counts including conspiracy, espionage, theft of classified information, and failing to register as agents of a foreign government. Both were convicted in May 1978 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia and sentenced in July 1978 to 15 years in prison. The case is often described as the only espionage case to come out of the Vietnam War, and the roughly year-long warrantless FBI surveillance that preceded the arrests produced the landmark "Truong doctrine" (United States v. Truong Dinh Hung, 629 F.2d 908 (4th Cir. 1980)); the Supreme Court declined to hear the final appeal in January 1982. Humphrey began serving his sentence in 1982 and was paroled in 1986. Sympathetic accounts at the time — including a 1982 Sojourners article titled "Scapegoated" — portrayed him as a man punished for trying to rescue his family.
profiles.finding: Sojourners Scapegoated1982 and Columbia Missourian1978 corroborate USIA identity. Football player1969, recent obituary, speaker and military photographs rejected.

profiles.name: Al Larcinese
profiles.description:
On December 12, 1977, U.S. District Judge John Feikens sentenced seven auto workers — "the Trenton 7" — to a week in federal prison for criminal contempt of a restraining order barring picketing at Chrysler's Trenton Engine Plant (UAW Local 372) in Trenton, Michigan. During the brutal heat wave of the summer of 1977, thousands of Detroit-area auto workers had walked out of plants where temperatures reached 120–130°F; at the Trenton plant, the firing of several union stewards over one such heat walkout triggered a week-long wildcat strike. Of the hundreds of workers who picketed, seven were singled out for prosecution. Although nearly 60 workers fired for heat walkouts at other Detroit-area plants were rehired in a Chrysler–UAW deal, the Trenton 7 were not reinstated and were instead tried without a jury and convicted. Supporters denounced the case as a frame-up and an assault on the right to strike.

Al Larcinese was one of the seven defendants, who likened the prosecution to the labor repression of the 1930s.
profiles.finding: Workers Vanguard September30 1977 reports Trenton workers and Al Larcinese; inspect photo caption before adoption.

profiles.name: Cecil E. Rust
profiles.description:
The pressmen's strike against The Washington Post began before dawn on October 1, 1975, when members of Local 6 of the International Printing and Graphic Communications Union disabled all 72 of the paper's press units and beat the night foreman, James Hover. The Post hired permanent replacements, broke the union, and the District's pressmen voted to decertify Local 6 in March 1977 — a landmark defeat for organized labor. A federal grand jury indicted fifteen pressmen over the pressroom violence, while none of the workers who crossed the picket line and clashed with strikers were charged; supporters denounced the prosecutions as a selective, union-busting "frame-up" that drained the local's resources through legal-defense costs. Fourteen pressmen pleaded guilty in April 1977 to misdemeanors — ranging from disorderly conduct to simple assault — after prosecutors dropped the felony charges, and were sentenced on May 19, 1977 by D.C. Superior Court Judge Sylvia Bacon, who declared that "the existence of a labor dispute or a strike does not justify violence." Their sentences were met with protest rallies outside the courthouse.

Cecil E. Rust was sentenced to 120 days in the District's work-release program, plus a suspended jail term and one year's probation. In a sentencing memorandum, prosecutors described Rust and Eugene O'Sullivan as "the leaders and catalysts for the violence, damage and destruction."

profiles.finding: Workers Vanguard June3 1977 confirms Cecil Rust120days. Rev Cecil Timothy Rust obituary and Air Force donor names not matched.

Jack D. McIntosh received the stiffest sentence of the group — two concurrent one-year jail terms. He had pleaded guilty to destruction of property in the pressroom and was separately convicted by a jury of assaulting former Washington Post reporter Jules Witcover (later a syndicated columnist). Prosecutors said McIntosh played a significant role in disabling the presses, and he was required to serve at least four months before becoming eligible for parole.

profiles.name: John H. Raffo
profiles.description:
The pressmen's strike against The Washington Post began before dawn on October 1, 1975, when members of Local 6 of the International Printing and Graphic Communications Union disabled all 72 of the paper's press units and beat the night foreman, James Hover. A federal grand jury indicted fifteen pressmen over the pressroom violence, while none of the workers who crossed the picket line and clashed with strikers were charged; supporters denounced the prosecutions as a selective, union-busting "frame-up" that drained the local's resources through legal-defense costs. Fourteen pressmen pleaded guilty in April 1977 to misdemeanors — ranging from disorderly conduct to simple assault — after prosecutors dropped the felony charges, and were sentenced on May 19, 1977 by D.C. Superior Court Judge Sylvia Bacon, who declared that "the existence of a labor dispute or a strike does not justify violence." Their sentences were met with protest rallies outside the courthouse.

John H. Raffo was sentenced to 120 days in the District's work-release program, plus a suspended jail term and one year's probation.

profiles.name: Anna Gyorgy
profiles.description: Montague Farm activist who in 1974 helped organize the Alternative Energy Coalition in Montague, Mass., and in 1976 was part of the founding coalition of the Clamshell Alliance. Authored the influential 1979 reference book "No Nukes: Everyone's Guide to Nuclear Power" (South End Press), which became the movement's bible. Since 1985 has lived in Ireland, West Africa and Germany, continuing international ecofeminist and anti-nuclear organizing.
